name: Tomas Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the children's ward at a district hospital, so it's everything from asthma and bronchiolitis to kids after appendix surgery. A shift is obs, meds, feeds, calming parents, and a lot of distraction work, blowing bubbles while the doctor puts a line in. I like the kids, they're honest. What wears me out is the parents who are scared and take it out on you, and the drug calculations, because children's doses are all by weight and I'm still slow at them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you get back?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Hannah. She teaches Year 3 at a primary school across town. We rent a two-bed terrace and we're saving for a deposit, we've got about five months of costs put away, which sounds good until you look at house prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fair enough, I can believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the NHS has bigger things to fix first, like the number of nurses and the waiting lists. I'd probably say it with a bit of a laugh, because every year somebody promises the computer will fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much for me. Kids keep getting chest infections and breaking arms on trampolines, so a children's nurse isn't going anywhere in this picture. Hannah's job is safe too. The only stress is getting a house before prices run away from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd finish my paediatric competencies, keep putting about three hundred a month toward the deposit with Hannah, and maybe use AI now and then to tidy up my reflective writing for revalidation, which is the paperwork you do to stay registered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit impatient about the house, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small terrace near Hannah's school, so she can walk. Something like ours, but ours. We'd need about another eight thousand for the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock that plan off course, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rate rise, or one of us getting ill. Or Hannah's school getting merged, they keep talking about that. But nothing to do with computers.

say: The NHS has bigger things to fix, like **nurse numbers**.
I'd **laugh** at the yearly promise that computers will fix everything.
think: A **children's nurse** isn't going anywhere in this picture.
The only real stress is getting **a house** before prices run away.
do: Save about **£300 a month** with Hannah for a deposit.
Use AI now and then for **revalidation** writing.
feel: **Calm**, if a bit impatient about buying a house.
S0.quote: Kids keep getting chest infections and breaking arms on trampolines, so a children's nurse isn't going anywhere in this picture.
fieldNote: Two **steady incomes** make him genuinely calm here.
His main goal is a **house deposit**, about £8,000 short.
He uses AI **occasionally**, for tidy-up tasks only.

steps.text: Finish the paediatric competencies on the children's ward
Save about £300 a month with Hannah for the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking and booking. Some of that's my day too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for the admin side. Software can write the discharge letter, but no software is going to hold a screaming toddler still for a cannula. I'd say that in the staff room and probably to my mates at five-a-side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine but things would shift around me. The ward clerk might go, the bed managers would change. And Hannah's school would probably start using AI for lesson plans and marking, which she'd half like and half hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools once a couple of the other nurses had tried them and said they were safe, especially for checking doses. I'd keep saving for the house, but I'd want a slightly bigger cushion first, maybe six months instead of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. My job's safe. It's the world around it shifting that I'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust an AI to check a child's drug dose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As a second check, yes, after it's proven. Never instead of a second nurse. Not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah about her marking going to AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say take the free time and don't let them fill it with more meetings. She'd laugh, because they always fill it with meetings.

No software can **hold a toddler** still for a cannula.
think: I'd be fine, but the **ward clerk** and bed managers would change.

do: Use AI **dose checking** once colleagues say it's safe.
Grow our cushion from five to **six months** before buying.
feel: A little **uneasy**, noticing the world shifting around a safe job.
S1.quote: Software can write the discharge letter, but no software is going to hold a screaming toddler still for a cannula.
fieldNote: He's **pragmatic**: AI as a second check, never a replacement.
He waits for **proof** from colleagues before adopting tools.
He stretches the **cushion** slightly before committing to a mortgage.

steps.text: Use AI dose checking as a second check once colleagues approve
Build savings to six months before applying for a mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before we'd even have the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from the government, not panic. Help for people whose jobs go, retraining that's real. I wouldn't get angry about it online. I'd just say: sort it out, sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my girlfriend teaches seven-year-olds and I nurse them, and by 2031 both of our jobs could be up for grabs. The thinking part of Hannah's job is huge, lesson planning, marking, reports. Mine's more hands-on, so I'd get until about 2031 before robots could do the obs and feeds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the house on hold and keep the deposit money as a safety net. I'd do a course in something that's hard to automate, maybe neonatal care, where it's tiny babies and very skilled hands. I'd start using the AI tools properly, since they'd be everywhere anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Both of us in the firing line, just at different times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a team, and the deposit isn't going anywhere, it just becomes our emergency fund. She'd be more scared than me, I think, because hers comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want kids, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Maybe later. That's the honest answer. We'd talked about 2029, now maybe 2031 or after.

say: We need a **proper plan** from government, not panic.
Help people whose jobs go with **real retraining**, and sort it out sensibly.
think: Hannah's **teaching job** and my nursing job could both go by 2031.
My **hands-on work** buys me about three extra years.
do: Put the **house purchase** on hold and keep the deposit as a safety net.
feel: **Anxious**, with both of them in the firing line at different times.
S2.quote: My girlfriend teaches seven-year-olds and I nurse them, and by 2031 both of our jobs could be up for grabs.
fieldNote: He sees Hannah's job hit **first**, because it's heavy on thinking work.
He'd **delay children** to around 2031 or later.
His centre view shows in wanting a **sensible plan**, not protest.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold for now
Keep the deposit money as an emergency fund
Apply for a neonatal intensive care course
Start using the ward's AI charting and dose tools daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but there's room to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: sensible plan, real retraining, don't panic. Maybe a bit more upbeat, because there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes the order. With five years' warning, the house can wait a year and the course can't. I'd do the neonatal course first, while Hannah looks at what teaching looks like after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the neonatal course in 2027. We'd keep saving for the house, but look at smaller places. I'd use AI tools once they're common on the ward, and probably push Hannah to try them early too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe a touch anxious. We'd have a plan, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a smaller place mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A one-bed flat, probably, instead of the terrace. Hannah would hate it. I'd say it's sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a touch anxious'. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest, because Hannah's job still goes before mine. But we'd be ready, which helps.

say: We need a **sensible plan** and real retraining, without panic.
Five years gives everyone **time to think**, so I'd sound more upbeat.
think: With five years' warning, the **neonatal course** comes before the house.
Hannah's **teaching job** still goes before mine, which is the real worry.

feel: **Anxious** but ready, because they'd have a plan.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, the house can wait a year and the course can't.
fieldNote: He **reorders priorities**: course first, house later.
He admits real **anxiety** once pressed on Hannah's job.
He's **steady**, adopting tools once they're common on the ward.

steps.text: Start a neonatal intensive care course in 2027

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be smart about it: plan, retrain, look after people. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means we could buy the house, maybe have a kid, and still be ready. I'd rather buy a smaller flat in 2029 than a nice house in 2027 that we can't afford in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the neonatal course around 2028, buy a small flat around 2029, and keep saving. I'd use AI tools as they come in. Hannah would have time to move into something like special needs teaching, where there's more hands-on care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Ten years is enough to feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why special needs teaching for Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's done a placement in it and loved it. It's very hands-on, lots of one-to-one, so the robots would be later there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rates and house prices, honestly. Same as now. AI's a long way off in this picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hannah's job goes almost straight away and mine follows three years later. What would help is honest guidance about which nursing jobs will still exist, and help paying for courses into those areas.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people actually need to hear. I don't need anyone to tell me robots are coming. I need someone to tell me which nurses will still be needed when they get here.

headlineQuote: I don't need anyone to tell me robots are coming. I need someone to tell me which nurses will still be needed when they get here.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on a children's ward, still slow at weight-based drug doses.
He rents with his girlfriend Hannah, a **primary teacher**, and they have about five months saved.
He's **pragmatic**, adopting AI once colleagues prove it safe.
His mood turns **anxious** when Hannah's thinking-heavy job looks set to go first.
His plans centre on **neonatal care** training and a house deposit he'd delay if needed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Hannah's job goes first and his follows within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest guidance** about which nursing jobs will still exist.
Help **paying for courses** into those areas.
